candidate_sources.title: Oak Anthracnose : Landscape : Center for Agriculture, Food, and the Environment (CAFE) at UMass Amherst
candidate_sources.snippet: Symptoms first appear as water-soaked, blighted leaf margins or as blotches along primary veins as new foliage develops. Over time, lesions become dry, papery and gray-colored. Pubescent leaves can become distorted or shriveled and may be shed prematurely. Caused by Apiognomonia errabunda (previously Discula quercina). The fungus overwinters in leaf debris, twigs, stems and cankers; wet rainy weather favors infection during bud break.

candidate_sources.title: Oak: Anthracnose | Hortsense | Washington State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Oak anthracnose causes small to large brown lesions on the leaves, usually along the midrib or main veins. Young leaves may be severely deformed by infections occurring during development. Cool, wet spring weather favors disease.

candidate_sources.title: Apiognomonia errabunda (anthracnose) | CABI Datasheet
candidate_sources.snippet: Datasheet on Apiognomonia errabunda, the fungal pathogen causing anthracnose on oak (Quercus) and other broadleaf trees. Anamorph Discula umbrinella. Covers host range, distribution, symptoms, biology and disease cycle.

candidate_sources.title: Oak (Quercus spp.)-Anthracnose | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Oak is infected by Apiognomonia quercina, anamorph Discula quercina. Symptoms include leaf lesions along veins, defoliation and twig dieback. Includes cultural and chemical management recommendations.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Leaf Scorch on Oaks | Texas Plant Disease Diagnostic Lab
candidate_sources.snippet: Typical symptoms of bacterial leaf scorch on oaks include premature browning, or scorching of leaves often accompanied by a yellow border separating the green and brown tissue. Caused by Xylella fastidiosa, the tree will eventually die, usually within 4-5 years of the initial appearance of symptoms. Can be confused with abiotic stresses and oak wilt.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Leaf Scorch on Oak (John W. Howard II and Peng Tian) | University of Missouri Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Bacterial leaf scorch on oak. Symptoms in oak are characterized by dead margins with green tissues near the main veins and leaf petiole. Symptoms first appear in late summer in individual branches; the following spring, affected branches refoliate and leaves remain green until scorch symptoms reappear. Caused by Xylella fastidiosa, spread by sharpshooters and spittlebugs.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Leaf Scorch of Trees | University of Maryland Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Bacterial leaf scorch is caused by Xylella fastidiosa, a bacterium limited within the plant to the water-conducting tissue (xylem). It affects shade trees including elm, oak, sycamore, maple, mulberry, and sweetgum. Symptoms include premature browning or scorching of leaves with a yellow border separating green and brown tissue. There are no treatments; prune symptomatic branches and dead wood promptly.

candidate_sources.title: Oak - Botryosphaeria Canker - Cooperative Extension: Insect Pests, Ticks and Plant Diseases - University of Maine Cooperative Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Oak Botryosphaeria canker. Botryosphaeria species cause oak branch canker and dieback. Symptoms include scattered branch dieback, eruptive cankers on the bark, sunken lesions on branches, and black fungal fruiting structures (pycnidia). The fungi infect through wounds and stressed tissue.

candidate_sources.title: Botryosphaeria Canker and Dieback of Trees and Shrubs in the Landscape | VCE Publications | Virginia Tech
candidate_sources.snippet: Symptoms of Botryosphaeria cankers and dieback are most commonly seen as wilting or dieback of branches on an otherwise healthy tree. Typical symptoms include thinning canopies, browning and prematurely shedding foliage, scattered branch dieback, eruptive cankers, gummosis, blisters, and black pycnidia. Botryosphaeria fungi are opportunistic pathogens that overwinter as fruiting bodies on dead tissue and infect through wounds and stress.

candidate_sources.title: Botryosphaeria Dieback/Canker (Botryosphaeria dothidea) - Hort Answers - University of Illinois Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Botryosphaeria Dieback/Canker is caused by the fungus Botryosphaeria dothidea. The pathogen causes sunken cankers, branch dieback, and discolored bark on a wide range of woody hosts including oak. Cankers can coalesce to girdle shoots and branches; black fruiting bodies form on infected bark.

candidate_sources.title: Coryneum Twig Canker on Southern Live Oak in Florida
candidate_sources.snippet: In May 2001, following several years of severe drought, a depressed twig canker was observed on southern live oak (Quercus virginiana) in central Florida, with disease symptoms including twig and branch canker and dieback, distortion of young leaves, and premature leaf drop. Coryneum japonicum was associated with the cankers, and the fungus produced abundant, subepidermal, dark brown, linearly arranged acervuli on affected tissues.
diseases_mentioned: twig and branch canker and dieback

candidate_sources.title: Coryneum Twig Canker on Southern Live Oak in Florida - PubMed
candidate_sources.snippet: Coryneum Twig Canker on Southern Live Oak in Florida. A depressed twig canker associated with Coryneum japonicum was observed on southern live oak (Quercus virginiana), with symptoms of twig and branch canker, dieback, distortion of young leaves, and premature leaf drop.

candidate_sources.title: Oak Twig Blight / Home and Landscape / UC Statewide IPM Program (UC IPM)
candidate_sources.snippet: The fungus sporadically causes twig blight (dieback) in coast live oak, interior live oak, and valley oak. Trees with heavy infestations become unsightly and lose vigor.

candidate_sources.title: Oak (Quercus spp.)-Cytospora Canker | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Portions of the branch die and may develop small pimple-like fruiting bodies (pycnidia) of the fungus. The OSU Plant Clinic has found Cytospora sp. on submitted oak samples. The fungus is opportunistic and quick to attack plants predisposed by heat, drought, winter damage, or infection by other pathogens. Management: Prune out and destroy affected limbs.

candidate_sources.title: Leucostoma and Valsa (Cytospora) Cankers - Bugwoodwiki
candidate_sources.snippet: Valsa and Leucostoma, often referred to as Cytospora cankers, affect many species of trees including alder, aspen, cottonwood, poplar, elm, willow, birch, maple, ash, sycamore, mulberry, oak, apple, stone fruits, and spruce. Cankers on branches/trunk differ in color; small black pimple-like fruiting structures appear, and orange spirals of spores emerge during wet conditions.

candidate_sources.title: Cytospora Canker - CSU Extension - Colorado State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Cytospora canker is caused by fungi in the genus Cytospora. The first noticeable symptom is usually wilting or flagging of a branch, with a dark-colored bark canker with a depressed center. Cytospora canker can be distinguished from other cankers by the presence of pycnidia, pimple-like structures on the outer bark.

candidate_sources.title: Oak (Quercus spp.)-Ganoderma Root and Butt Rot | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Oak (Quercus spp.)-Ganoderma Root and Butt Rot. Cause: Ganoderma species, fungi that cause a white rot decay of the roots and butt (lower trunk). The fungus enters through wounds. Decay is a white-mottled rot of the trunk and large roots; the conk (fruiting body) appears at the base of the tree.

candidate_sources.title: Root and Butt Rot caused by Ganoderma sessile : Landscape : Center for Agriculture, Food, and the Environment (CAFE) at UMass Amherst
candidate_sources.snippet: Ganoderma sessile (previously known as G. lucidum) is one of the most common root and butt rot pathogens in the northeast. Oaks, maples, beech and honeylocust are primary hosts. Decay is a white-mottled rot of the trunk and large roots. Perennial woody conks appear on the base of the tree or on trunk wounds, grey-to-brown on top with a pure white underside.

candidate_sources.title: Root and Butt Rots of Hardwood Trees | Yard and Garden (Iowa State University Extension)
candidate_sources.snippet: Ganoderma applanatum (Artist's conk) and other Ganoderma species are common root and butt rot fungi on oaks and other hardwoods. Affected trees show yellowing, wilting or undersized leaves, dead branches and are easily blown down. The presence of a conk at the base of a tree is a sign of infection.

candidate_sources.title: Ganoderma rot | Texas Plant Disease Diagnostic Lab
candidate_sources.snippet: Ganoderma rot is a white rot of the roots and lower trunk of many hardwood trees including oak. The fungus produces a shelf-like conk at the base of the tree and causes decay that weakens the tree and predisposes it to failure.

candidate_sources.title: Tubakia (Actinopelte) Leaf Spot â€“ Wisconsin Horticulture
candidate_sources.snippet: Circular leaf spots ranging from Â¼ - Â½ inch in diameter and red-brown to black in color, often surrounded by a chlorotic halo. Spots can fuse into larger blotches; vein infection leads to collapse of leaf tissue. Caused by the fungus Tubakia dryina (formerly Actinopelte dryina). Symptoms develop mid- to late summer. Management focuses on raking/destroying fallen leaves and improving air movement rather than fungicides.

candidate_sources.title: Tubakia leaf spot in Oaks | Yard and Garden â€“ Iowa State University Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Tubakia leaf spot of oaks, caused by Tubakia dryina, produces dark brown to reddish-brown circular spots on leaves in mid- to late summer. Spotting on veins causes collapse of leaf tissue beyond the infection point and can lead to premature defoliation. Oaks in the red oak group are most susceptible. Management includes sanitation of fallen leaves.

candidate_sources.title: Tubakia leaf spot of oak - MSU Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Tubakia leaf spot, caused by the fungus Tubakia dryina (formerly Actinopelte dryina), produces large, circular, nickel-sized necrotic brown spots on oak foliage. The fungus overwinters in infected twigs and dead leaves and spreads by wind and rain splash. Symptoms appear mid- to late summer, unlike oak anthracnose. The disease is aesthetic and will not cause tree death.

candidate_sources.title: Oak | Texas Plant Disease Handbook
candidate_sources.snippet: Information about various oak leaf diseases including fungal leaf spots that form brown, irregular spots following leaf veins and midrib, with a papery texture after drying; large leaf spot caused by Monochaetia desmazierii causes 2-inch circular spots with yellowish centers and reddish-brown margins on red and white oaks.
diseases_mentioned: Monochaetia leaf spot / large leaf spot (Monochaetia desmazierii)

candidate_sources.title: Florida Oak Tree Diseases - Garden Guides
candidate_sources.snippet: Large leaf spot is caused by the fungus Monochaetia desmazierii and infects the leaves of red and white oaks. The disease causes 2-inch circular spots with yellowish centers and reddish-brown margins to form on leaves, and when the disease progresses, rings form around the spots, becoming target-like.

candidate_sources.title: The large leaf spot of chestnut and oak associated with Monochaetia desmazierii
candidate_sources.snippet: The large leaf spot associated with M. desmazierii is reported to occur in the U.S.A. on Acer rubrum, Castanea dentata, Hamamelis virginiana, 4 species of Hicoria, 10 species of Quercus, and Ulmus alata.
diseases_mentioned: Large leaf spot of chestnut and oak (Monochaetia desmazierii)

candidate_sources.title: Key to Diseases of Oaks in the Landscape | UGA Cooperative Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: A diagnostic key to landscape oak diseases covering leaf spots, oak leaf blister, anthracnose, and oak wilt, with symptom descriptions and management guidance for fungal leaf diseases of Quercus species.

candidate_sources.title: Oak (Quercus spp.)-Nectria Canker | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Neonectria ditissima (formerly Nectria galligena), a fungus, occasionally causes a perennial target-shaped canker on the trunk and limbs of Oregon white oak. The canker initially appears as a slightly sunken oval or round lesion; repeated fungus growth and callus formation give the canker a target appearance with concentric rings. Pruning wounds or other mechanical injury serve as entry points.

candidate_sources.title: Nectria Canker | Diseases of Forest and Shade Trees (University of Minnesota)
candidate_sources.snippet: Nectria canker is caused by the fungus Neonectria galligena. It produces perennial target-shaped cankers on the stems and branches of many hardwood trees including oak. Clusters of fungal fruiting bodies (sporodochia and perithecia) erupt from the bark in spring and summer.

candidate_sources.title: Nectria Canker | UC Statewide IPM Program (UC IPM)
candidate_sources.snippet: Nectria fungi infect woody species through weakened or wounded tissue, such as leaf scars and pruning wounds. Spherical orange or red sporodochia and perithecia (coral spots) about 1/50 to 1/16 inch in diameter erupt from bark. Trees with stem cankers are subject to breakage when the canker affects more than 30% to 40% of the stem diameter. Proper cultural care is the most important management method.

candidate_sources.title: Nectria Canker | Center for Agriculture, Food, and the Environment (UMass Amherst)
candidate_sources.snippet: Nectria canker is caused by Neonectria galligena and Neonectria cinnabarina. Branch lesions may appear sunken or water-soaked; over time cankers with cracking, splitting and sloughing bark develop. Orange- to pink-colored pads of fungal tissue erupt through the bark. Nectria canker is incurable, but removing branches with cankers can help slow the spread.

candidate_sources.title: Oak Leaf Blister - Penn State Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Oak leaf blister is caused by the fungus Taphrina caerulescens. Symptoms appear as raised, blistered, greenish-yellow spots on upper leaf surfaces and darker, corresponding sunken spots on lower leaf surfaces. Incidence is favored by cool, wet spring conditions. Chemical control is rarely necessary.

candidate_sources.title: Oak Leaf Blister | Yard and Garden - Iowa State University Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Oak leaf blister, caused by Taphrina caerulescens, infects about 50 species of oak. Symptoms are raised or sunken lesions resembling blisters, lighter green than the rest of the leaf, ranging 1/4"-1/2" in diameter, eventually turning brown. Remove fallen infected leaves to reduce infection.

candidate_sources.title: Oak Leaf Blister (Taphrina caerulescens) - Hort Answers - University of Illinois Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Symptoms appear early in summer as blisters, bulges or depressions on the upper leaf surface, with the lower side turning grayish. Blistered areas may merge and change color from yellow to brown, causing leaf distortion. The fungus overwinters in buds and infects young emerging leaves after bud break under cool, moist conditions.

candidate_sources.title: Oak Leaf Blister - UMass Amherst Center for Agriculture, Food, and the Environment
candidate_sources.snippet: Oak leaf blister is a foliar disease of oak caused by the fungus Taphrina caerulescens. Spores are dispersed in spring and infect newly emerging leaves just after bud break. Mature leaves are usually resistant to infection.

candidate_sources.title: Oak wilt in Minnesota | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Oak wilt is caused by Bretziella fagacearum, a fungus that develops in the xylem, the water-carrying cells of trees. Oak wilt kills trees by preventing the movement of water and sugars to the crown, causing leaves to wilt and die. The fungus is spread between trees by small beetles or root grafts. Management includes severing root grafts, fungicide treatments, and avoiding pruning in spring and early summer.

candidate_sources.title: Oak Wilt | Ohioline - The Ohio State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Oak wilt, caused by the fungus Bretziella fagacearum (formerly Ceratocystis fagacearum), is a serious fatal disease of oak trees. Red group oaks (pointed leaf tips) die much faster than white group oaks. Symptoms include wilt and browning beginning from leaf margins and progressing inward. Dead trees may develop spore mats that rupture the bark and smell sweet, attracting sap-feeding beetles.

candidate_sources.title: Oak Wilt | Yard and Garden - Iowa State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Oak wilt is a fatal disease of oak trees caused by the fungus Bretziella fagacearum. The fungus blocks the water-conducting vessels; symptoms include leaf yellowing, browning, wilt, and branch dieback. Red oaks are very susceptible and can die within 4-6 weeks, while white and bur oaks develop symptoms slowly. Spread occurs via beetles, root grafts, and movement of firewood.

candidate_sources.title: Oak Wilt (Ceratocystis fagacearum) - Hort Answers - University of Illinois Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Oak Wilt (Ceratocystis fagacearum). The outside of the leaves turn bronze, brown, or dull green, usually starting at the top of the leaf, while the base remains green. Some leaves curl, droop and wilt. The outermost ring of sapwood sometimes turns brown and appears as streaks when bark is peeled, or as a ring in cross-section.

candidate_sources.title: Bretziella fagacearum (previously Ceratocystis fagacearum) Oak Wilt - Fact Sheet | inspection.canada.ca
candidate_sources.snippet: Oak wilt is caused by the fungus Bretziella fagacearum, previously known as Ceratocystis fagacearum. The fungus invades the xylem and is spread by sap-feeding beetles and root grafts. All oak species are susceptible; red oaks are most severely affected.

candidate_sources.title: Inonotus Dryadeus â€“ butt and root rot of oaks â€“ Purdue Landscape Report
candidate_sources.snippet: Wood decay is a white-mottled rot generally confined to the large roots and the base of the tree near ground level. Annual conks appear on the base of the tree or large roots at ground level in summer and early autumn. Conks are large (7 inches or more) with numerous droplets of clear-yellow liquid on top. Trees may not show external symptoms while root rot decays the support structure, eventually leading to unexpected failure. Management options are limited; avoid wounding the tree.
diseases_mentioned: Inonotus dryadeus butt and root rot

candidate_sources.title: Root and Butt Rot caused by Bondarzewia berkeleyi (Berkeley's Polypore) â€“ UMass Amherst CAFE
candidate_sources.snippet: Bondarzewia berkeleyi, known as Berkeley's polypore, primarily occurs on oak (Quercus) but also on chestnut, maple, and cherry. It causes a white stringy rot of the primary lateral roots and heartwood in the lower trunk, typically not extending beyond 3-5 feet. Most damaging to older, mature trees exposed to wounds. Confirmed by its distinctive fruiting bodies; oaks with conks are often extensively decayed with elevated failure rate.

candidate_sources.title: Secondary Wood-Rotting Pathogens of Stressed Oaks â€“ UMass Amherst CAFE
candidate_sources.snippet: As trees age, compounding stresses such as insect defoliation and drought weaken natural defenses, leaving oaks susceptible to infection by root and butt rot fungi. Wood decay symptoms include discoloration of wood, alteration of strength properties, and formation of cavities. These polypore fungi attack older, wounded trees and can lead to structural failure.

candidate_sources.title: Oak (Quercus spp.)-Inonotus Root and Butt Rot â€“ Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Sparse foliage with limb dieback may be symptomatic but is not consistently associated with the disease. Wood decay is a white-mottled rot generally confined to the large roots and the base of the tree near ground level. Annual conks form at the base in summer and early autumn. Management: avoid wounding; irrigation water should not wet trunks; mowing equipment should not injure roots, crown, or lower trunk.
